analysis.one_liner: Slashes power plant nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide pollution that causes acid rain, using tradeable permits.
analysis.headline: The Acid Deposition Control Act, backed by a bipartisan group of 16 House members, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national permit program requiring electric utilities to cut nitrogen oxide emissions 70% below 1990 levels and halve sulfur dioxide allowances starting in 2005. It would have required industrial plants to install continuous pollution monitors, imposed penalties for excess emissions, set up a path toward controlling mercury from power plants, and required the EPA to report on whether the cuts were enough to protect ecosystems like the Adirondacks and Chesapeake Bay. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, especially in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic: the bill cited rising acidity in Adirondack lakes, damage to the Chesapeake Bay and other waterways, and fine-particle and ozone pollution linked to premature death and respiratory illness [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill stated as its purpose reducing utility nitrogen oxide emissions by 70% from 1990 levels and sulfur dioxide by 50% after the Clean Air Act's phase II requirements, citing scientific findings that these pollutants cause acid deposition, fine particulates suspected of causing significant mortality and illness, and ozone far from the emitting source [S2][S3].

It required the EPA to set ecosystem protection objectives for sensitive regions including the Adirondacks, Mid-Appalachian and Blue Ridge Mountains, the Great Lakes, Lake Champlain, Long Island Sound, and the Chesapeake Bay, and to tighten regulations by 2010 if the emissions cuts proved insufficient [S2][S3].

It required industrial facilities to install continuous emissions monitoring for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, opacity, and flow, and directed the EPA toward reporting requirements and controls for mercury emissions from large combustion units, a toxic pollutant that accumulates in fish [S2][S3].
Penalties were set at $12,000 per ton of unallowed emissions, inflation-adjusted, with facilities required to offset excess emissions two-for-one the following year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities, particularly coal- and oil-fired plants in the Midwest and South that would have had to cut emissions or buy allowances, and their customers, who could see some of those compliance costs passed through in electricity rates. The bill explicitly preserved state authority over utility rates [S3].

drawbacks.text: As a cap-and-trade program, it let a plant keep emitting by buying allowances from cleaner facilities, so some local communities could still face concentrated pollution even as regional totals fell; the bill text allows full transferability of allowances among facilities and any person [S3].

Allowances were allocated to states in proportion to their share of total electric power generated, and undistributed reserve allowances were auctioned with proceeds returned to affected source owners rather than to the public, meaning polluting generators received a valuable asset alongside their new obligations [S2][S3].

Compliance costs for cutting nitrogen oxide 70% and sulfur dioxide 50% would likely be passed at least partly into electricity prices, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge; the bill's own savings provisions left state utility rate regulation untouched [S3].

The mercury provisions were cautious: controls were required only after a study, a report, and monitoring regulations, and the regulations were directed to take technological feasibility and cost into account [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and ecosystem stakes were large: the bill's findings cited acidic Adirondack lakes increasing by up to 40% by 2040 without action and fine-particle pollution linked to significant mortality [S3]. The costs fell on a concentrated set of utilities and were designed to be reduced through trading, while the benefits — fewer premature deaths, cleaner lakes and coastal waters — accrued broadly to the public. The main design weaknesses were the trading system's potential for local pollution hot spots and allowances handed to generators at no charge.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee in early 1999, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative John Sweeney, a New York Republican, introduced the Acid Deposition Control Act on February 9, 1999, joined by New York colleagues including both parties' members, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1][S4][S5].

On March 1, 1999, the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment, which is where legislation on air pollution typically gets its first detailed consideration [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor debate — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].
The cosponsor list of 15 included 10 Democrats and 5 Republicans, almost all from New York, the state whose Adirondack lakes were a central stated beneficiary of the emission cuts [S2][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired utilities, which would have faced a 70% nitrogen oxide cut and deeper sulfur dioxide limits, avoided those compliance costs because the bill never advanced. Downwind states and damaged ecosystems got no new federal protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired utilities avoided new emission cuts

for.name: Rep. John E. Sweeney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial group of New York cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 10 House Democrats (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Towns, McNulty, Nadler, Hinchey, LaFalce, Ackerman, Lowey, and Maloney of New York.

for.name: 5 House Republicans (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. McHugh, Walsh, Lazio, Houghton, and others, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Commerce Committee (Chair Thomas Bliley)
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its February 1999 referral without holding a markup or advancing it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment (Chair Michael Bilirakis)
against.role: Subcommittee of referral; took no recorded action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 1, 1999, and no hearing, vote, or further action on it was ever recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but regionally concentrated: the sponsor was a Republican and cosponsors split 5 Republicans to 10 Democrats, overwhelmingly from New York, where acid rain damage to the Adirondacks was the driving concern [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required a 70% cut in nitrogen oxide emissions and halved sulfur dioxide allowances from 2005, with $12,000-per-ton penalties and mandatory continuous monitoring [S2][S3]. The design softened the blow — tradeable allowances, allocations proportional to power generation, and auction proceeds returned to source owners — but the net effect was a large compliance cost whose avoided burden was the public's health gain [S3].

industries.industry: Industrial boilers and large combustion facilities
industries.note: Facilities of 100 million Btu/hour or more would have had to install and operate continuous emissions monitoring systems, and large units would have faced mercury monitoring and eventual controls [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Emissions monitoring and control equipment makers
industries.note: The bill mandated continuous emissions monitoring systems on industrial facilities and directed the EPA toward mercury monitoring requirements, creating demand for monitoring hardware and services [S2][S3].
